content: Analysis of disease transmission and elimination can be conducted at lower administrative levels. This approach may allow for earlier declarations of transmission interruption and disease elimination. However, it is not recommended to proceed without proper evaluation by an internal team, as the number of assessments required at lower tiers could become overwhelming. Dr. Manoj Murhekar, Director of the National Institute of Epidemiology in Chennai, India, presented surveillance indicators used in tuberculosis (TB) control and the recommended process for verifying sub-national claims. This process involves reviewing programmatic data, such as TB scores, the number of cases requiring prophylactic treatment to prevent one case, medicine sales (both public and private), and community-based surveys. The National Tuberculosis Programme has set ambitious targets, including an 80% reduction in TB incidence by 2020 (compared to 2015), a 90% reduction in annual TB deaths by 2030, and ensuring no TB-affected households face catastrophic costs by 2020. Impact indicators include reducing TB incidence, prevalence, and mortality rates, as well as achieving zero catastrophic costs for TB-affected families. Monitoring progress toward a TB-free status at sub-national levels is critical. A system has been initiated to incentivize and reward high-performing districts or states. This includes estimating TB incidence and underreporting in the notification system (Nikshay). The sampling strategy involves dividing districts into survey units, selecting villages or wards based on population size, and identifying eligible individuals for sputum sample collection until 30 bacteriologically positive TB cases are found in each district. Community-based surveys use indicators such as the proportion of symptomatic participants eligible for sputum collection, incident cases identified during the survey, and underreporting of cases not found in Nikshay. Verification of sub-national TB-free claims is based on specific criteria. For example, claims are not recommended if any of the three incidence estimates exceed 10% of the baseline. Claims are supported if two out of three point estimates show a decline in incidence, and no estimate indicates an increase from the baseline. Higher-than-claimed categories are recommended if the lower bounds of confidence intervals support a greater decline in incidence. LTAS includes reviewing epidemiological data, assessing health facilities, validating data through field surveys, and verifying criteria. Epidemiological data is analyzed over 10–20 years, and health facility assessments verify the availability of diagnostic services, staff knowledge, and resources for managing ulcers, disabilities, stigma, and mental health. Field surveys involve sampling at-risk populations, including children, to detect leprosy cases. Verification of criteria is conducted by internal teams at sub-national levels, with LTAS serving as a pre-qualification tool for declaring transmission interruption. When all sub-national units within a jurisdiction achieve transmission interruption, the jurisdiction is automatically declared as having reached this milestone. Similarly, when all jurisdictions meet the criteria for disease elimination, the country is considered to have achieved elimination. Post-elimination surveillance is maintained for at least ten years to detect sporadic cases. An international team verifies disease elimination at the national level. A Country Dossier is prepared to document evidence of leprosy elimination at the national level. It includes epidemiological data, programmatic criteria, and achievements. The dossier is submitted to the World Health Organization (WHO) for verification. Supporting evidence includes trends in leprosy, program evolution, and surveillance mechanisms. Social determinants of health, such as literacy levels, economic conditions, and access to services, are also included. Information on the health system, including human resources, training facilities, and budget allocations, is provided to demonstrate sustainability and political commitment. Mandatory information on leprosy control activities includes the history of the program, case detection, treatment, and epidemiological data. The dossier also outlines sub-national assessments, classification of units by endemicity, and planning details such as strategic plans, standard operating procedures, and resource allocation. The LTAS protocol and reporting formats are developed to guide countries in assessing transmission interruption and disease elimination. Surveillance systems, including web-based reporting and mandatory notification of sporadic cases, are essential for monitoring progress. Research on seroprevalence of anti-M. leprae PGL-I IgM antibodies among children is recommended to assess community transmission. Countries are expected to conduct sub-national assessments and include reports in the national dossier. LTAS is recommended for internal assessments of transmission interruption and disease elimination at sub-national levels, with WHO verification at the national level. Technical guidance is provided on LTAS protocols, dossier preparation, and critical incident investigations for sporadic cases. Other considerations include zoonotic transmission of M. leprae from armadillos and leprosy caused by M. lepromatosis. Surveillance and response systems must be robust to achieve and sustain transmission interruption, disease elimination, and post-elimination surveillance.
